builder_plan.scenario: Possible product use: a SaaS data assistant that repeatedly looks up the same customer tables, then makes mistakes after a schema change.
builder_plan.change: Add a background memory checker to a sandbox copy of that assistant. Keep customer data and memory isolated. Give the checker only the read access needed to validate a record, and keep the current memory pipeline available as a fallback.
builder_plan.baseline: Run three conditions: no memory, your current memory, and the same memory with checking. Keep the answering model, tools, retrieval, and task order fixed.
steps: Prepare 30 representative database questions with verified answers. Change a table name or data convention halfway through the sandbox sequence. Define a spending limit and an acceptable failure rate before testing.
Run each condition from a fresh environment and empty memory. Let memory persist within a run, never between conditions. Hide future questions from the checker.

Repeat at least three paired runs with matching question orders. Record answering, distillation, checking, and retrieval usage separately. This pilot size is a Paperraft suggestion, not the paper's evaluation protocol.
Inspect wrong answers and the memory records that caused them. Save per-task results and check whether new records remain correct after the environment changes.
builder_plan.measure: Correct answers, unnecessary database calls, stale records, response latency, and total cost per successful task including failed attempts and all memory maintenance.
builder_plan.decision: Keep checking only if it improves your chosen quality target at an acceptable total cost. If your goal is savings, the reduction in answering cost must exceed the added checking and maintenance cost. Use paired results to inspect variation; three pilot runs are not proof of a stable production gain.

builder_review.intro: An assistant can remember yesterday's mistake as confidently as yesterday's useful discovery. This study checks candidate memories against the working environment before saving them. For a small product, the question is whether that extra check earns back its cost.
builder_review.mechanism: After a task ends, a separate curator checks proposed memories with read-only tools before saving or revising them. The responding agent and its memory reader stay the same. The added work happens during memory maintenance.
builder_review.takeaway: For an existing memory product, start with the comparison against ordinary memory. The no-memory headline includes the benefit of adding memory at all. The extra three percentage points do not establish a reliable product gain, and the reported task-agent bill leaves maintenance out.

comparisons.title: CLBench: the headline versus no memory
comparisons.definition: Pass rate is the share of database questions answered correctly.
comparisons.scope: 40 questions with a schema change halfway through; GPT-5.4; five paired runs.
comparisons.caveat: This compares the whole memory system against no memory. It does not isolate the value of probing.

comparisons.title: CLBench: the extra value of checking memory
comparisons.definition: Same pass metric, now against ordinary memory.
comparisons.scope: Same 40-question experiment. Reported 95% intervals are ±16 and ±5 percentage points.
comparisons.caveat: The intervals overlap. These means alone do not establish a reliable improvement from adding the checking step.

comparisons.title: CLBench: whose cost went down?
comparisons.definition: Task-agent spending for the 40-question run, averaged across runs.
comparisons.scope: Task-response phase only. Distillation and memory curation are excluded.
comparisons.caveat: This is not total operating cost or cost per request. Any extra maintenance cost must be counted before claiming savings.

title: Grounding Agent Memory: Environment-Probing Curation for Enterprise Agents
summary: The method replaces a post-task memory curator that works only from completed trajectories with one that has least-privilege, read-only environment tools to verify, scope, and refresh candidate memories, requiring no retraining and no changes to the task agent, retriever, or memory schema. Costs are an additional asynchronous curator stage with its own inference spend and tool-call latency, plus engineering effort to expose auditable read-only world tools; task-agent cost reportedly falls, but total pipeline cost rises. It can fail if probing tools return misleading or partial environment state, if read-only permissions are misconfigured into a security risk, and because results come from a single GHCP-based harness on database and consulting tasks, gains may not transfer to other agent stacks or domains.
rationale: The gains are large and deployment-compatible with API-based agents on constrained infrastructure, but the evidence is confined to one vendor harness and two task families, so the reader should validate on their own workload before production adoption.

exposure_map.finding: Minimum useful test: API or CPU. Published evidence: API or CPU.
Reported setup: standard Python, custom runtime.
Paperraft defines a 6-steps falsification test. No reproduction is recorded.

risks.statement: All evaluation is on two benchmarks via a GitHub Copilot SDK harness; gains may not transfer to other agent stacks or task distributions.

The improvement over plain memory is modest and confidence intervals overlap in places; in one of six APEX worlds probing was slightly worse, and the authors explicitly treat heterogeneity as unresolved.
Requires a safe, least-privilege read-only environment surface for the curator; without one it degenerates to trajectory-only curation, and granting such access has security/auditing implications.
Curator, distiller, and probe costs are excluded from reported task-agent cost; total system cost including curation is not the headline metric and could offset savings.
Probing adds asynchronous compute after every task; latency and cost of the curation phase at production scale are not quantified in the main results.
Results depend on specific frontier models (GPT-5.4, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7) and benchmark graders; weaker models may not probe effectively.

minimum_test: Pick one of your own workloads with a stream of 20-40 related tasks sharing latent environment structure (e.g., recurring database or document corpus), including at least one unannounced drift event, and define a strict pass/fail grader.

Stand up two memory pipelines that are identical in task agent, retriever, memory schema, distiller, and CRUD policy; give only one curator a least-privilege read-only subset of the environment tools plus the two probe prompt blocks from Appendix D.3.
Run both conditions plus a no-memory baseline on the same seeded task order with a small number of runs (at least 3 paired runs), keeping task agent, model, and prompts fixed.
Measure pass rate, task-agent tool calls, and task-agent cost, with curator/probe usage tracked separately; check whether probe curation calls stay read-only and off the task budget.

Inspect the committed memory records in both arms: if probed records are not more executable (explicit joins, paths, current schema) than trajectory-only records, the mechanism is not operating as claimed.
The reported gain is disproven for your workload if probing does not improve reward or tool-call count over trajectory-only memory, or if probing cost/latency erases the task-agent savings.
open_questions: What is the total end-to-end cost including distiller and curator/probe sessions, which the paper says are tracked separately but does not headline?
How many probe calls does the curator typically make per task, and what governance prevents read-only probes from leaking information or being abused?
Does the gain persist on non-benchmark, messier enterprise environments where read-only surfaces are incomplete?
How sensitive are results to the curator prompt and to the embedding retriever (intfloat/e5-base-v2)?
Would probing help when memory errors come from retrieval failure rather than record quality, which this design does not address?
